objectives: State why ATP is the energy currency and describe its synthesis and use.

blocks.title: ATP
blocks.md: **ATP** (adenosine triphosphate) is the immediate energy source of cells. Hydrolysis of ATP to ADP + Pᵢ releases a small, usable amount of energy; ATP is rebuilt by **phosphorylation** using energy from respiration or light. It is suitable because it is soluble, small, releases energy in manageable amounts and is quickly regenerated.

blocks.title: Glycolysis and the link reaction
blocks.md: **Glycolysis** (cytoplasm, no oxygen needed): glucose (6C) is phosphorylated using 2 ATP, split into two triose phosphates (3C), and oxidised to **2 pyruvate**, producing 4 ATP (net **2**) and **2 reduced NAD**. **Link reaction** (matrix): each pyruvate loses CO₂ and hydrogen to give **acetyl CoA** (2C) and reduced NAD.

blocks.caption: The four stages of aerobic respiration, where they occur and their main outputs.
blocks.alt: Four boxes in a vertical chain: glycolysis, link reaction, Krebs cycle and oxidative phosphorylation, with products written beside them.

blocks.title: Krebs cycle
blocks.md: Acetyl CoA (2C) joins oxaloacetate (4C) to make citrate (6C). Through a series of decarboxylation and dehydrogenation steps, citrate returns to oxaloacetate. **Per turn**: 2 CO₂, 3 reduced NAD, 1 reduced FAD and 1 ATP (substrate-level phosphorylation). The cycle turns **twice** per glucose.

blocks.title: Count per glucose, not per pyruvate
blocks.md: Because one glucose gives **two** pyruvate, the link reaction and the Krebs cycle each run **twice** per glucose. Per glucose, the totals before oxidative phosphorylation are 10 reduced NAD (2 + 2 + 6), 2 reduced FAD and 4 ATP (2 + 2). Many students forget to double the Krebs-cycle figures.

blocks.title: Worked example — reduced coenzymes
blocks.statement: Calculate the total number of reduced NAD and reduced FAD produced from one glucose molecule up to the end of the Krebs cycle.
steps: Glycolysis: 2 reduced NAD. Link: 2 reduced NAD (one per pyruvate). Krebs: 2 turns × 3 = 6.

blocks.title: Worked example — CO₂ released
blocks.statement: How many CO₂ molecules are released from one glucose molecule by the link reaction and the Krebs cycle?
steps: Link reaction: 1 CO₂ per pyruvate, so 2.
Krebs cycle: 2 CO₂ per turn × 2 turns = 4.
Total = 2 + 4 = 6, all six carbon atoms of glucose.

objectives: Explain the electron transport chain and chemiosmosis.

reviewNotes: Total ATP yield of 32 (2.5 and 1.5 per NAD/FAD) is the modern value; many Cameroonian textbooks still use 36–38. The teacher must decide which to teach.

Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Oxidative phosphorylation
blocks.md: Reduced NAD and reduced FAD deliver electrons to the **electron transport chain** on the **inner mitochondrial membrane**. As electrons pass along, energy is used to pump H⁺ from the matrix into the **intermembrane space**, creating a proton gradient. Protons flow back through **ATP synthase**, which makes ATP (**chemiosmosis**). **Oxygen** is the final electron acceptor and forms **water**.

blocks.title: ATP yield: which figure?
blocks.md: A modern estimate is about **2.5 ATP** per reduced NAD and **1.5 ATP** per reduced FAD. For one glucose: 10 reduced NAD → 25; 2 reduced FAD → 3; plus 4 by substrate-level phosphorylation = about **32 ATP**. Older textbooks give 36–38 because they used 3 and 2 ATP per NAD and FAD; always follow the figure taught in your course.

blocks.caption: Approximate ATP yield per glucose from each stage of aerobic respiration (modern figures).
blocks.alt: A bar chart with bars for glycolysis (2), Krebs cycle (2) and oxidative phosphorylation (28).

blocks.title: Anaerobic respiration
blocks.md: Without oxygen the chain stops and NAD is not re-oxidised. In **animals** pyruvate accepts hydrogen from reduced NAD to form **lactate** (the NAD can then be reused in glycolysis; lactate is later converted back in the liver). In **yeast and some plants** pyruvate is decarboxylated to ethanal and then reduced to **ethanol**. Only the 2 net ATP of glycolysis are made.

blocks.title: Respiratory quotient
blocks.md: RQ = volume of CO₂ produced ÷ volume of O₂ consumed. Carbohydrate: about 1.0; lipid: about 0.7; protein: about 0.8–0.9. RQ above 1 suggests anaerobic respiration.

blocks.title: Worked example — ATP yield
blocks.statement: Using 2.5 ATP per reduced NAD and 1.5 per reduced FAD, calculate the total ATP from one glucose (10 reduced NAD, 2 reduced FAD, 4 ATP by substrate-level phosphorylation).

blocks.title: Worked example — RQ of palmitic acid
blocks.statement: Palmitic acid is respired: C₁₆H₃₂O₂ + 23 O₂ → 16 CO₂ + 16 H₂O. Calculate RQ.

lessons.title: Photosynthesis: light-dependent and light-independent stages
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Respiration; photosynthesis (to be checked)

objectives: Describe the structure of the chloroplast and the role of pigments.
Describe the Calvin cycle and calculate ATP and NADPH requirements.
reviewNotes: Photosystem and carrier detail (Z-scheme) is simplified; check the depth expected.
3 ATP and 2 reduced NADP per CO₂ fixed is the standard school figure.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Overview
blocks.md: Photosynthesis converts light energy to chemical energy in organic molecules: 6CO₂ + 6H₂O → C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂. In the **chloroplast**, the **light-dependent stage** happens in the **thylakoid membranes** (grana) and the **light-independent stage (Calvin cycle)** in the **stroma**. Pigments (chlorophylls a and b, carotenoids) absorb mainly red and blue light; green light is reflected.

blocks.title: Light-dependent stage
blocks.md: Light excites electrons in **photosystems**; they pass along an electron transport chain, pumping H⁺ into the thylakoid space, and **ATP synthase** makes ATP (**photophosphorylation**). In **non-cyclic** photophosphorylation electrons are replaced by **photolysis** of water (H₂O → 2H⁺ + 2e⁻ + ½O₂) and finally reduce **NADP**. In **cyclic** photophosphorylation electrons return to photosystem I, making only ATP.

blocks.caption: The Calvin cycle in the stroma: carbon fixation, reduction and regeneration of RuBP.
blocks.alt: Four boxes around a ring: RuBP, CO₂ added by rubisco, two GP, and TP, joined by arrows.

blocks.title: Calvin cycle
blocks.md: CO₂ combines with **RuBP** (5C), catalysed by **rubisco**, to form two **GP** (3C). GP is reduced to **TP** (triose phosphate) using ATP and reduced NADP. Most TP is used to **regenerate RuBP** (needing ATP); the rest forms glucose, starch, amino acids and lipids. Six turns of the cycle fix 6 CO₂ and make one hexose.

blocks.title: Oxygen comes from water
blocks.md: The oxygen released in photosynthesis comes from **water** (photolysis), not from CO₂. The Calvin cycle is not 'dark': it uses ATP and reduced NADP made in the light, so it stops soon after light is removed. A common error is to say that 'light-independent' reactions can proceed at night indefinitely.

blocks.title: Worked example — ATP and NADPH per glucose
blocks.statement: Each turn of the Calvin cycle fixes one CO₂ and needs 3 ATP and 2 reduced NADP. How many ATP and reduced NADP are needed to make one hexose (six CO₂ fixed)?

blocks.title: Worked example — carbon counting
blocks.statement: Six molecules of RuBP combine with six CO₂. How many molecules of GP are formed, and how many carbon atoms do they contain?
steps: Each RuBP + CO₂ gives 2 GP, so 6 × 2 = 12 GP.

lessons.title: Limiting factors in photosynthesis
lessons.programRef: GCE A Level Biology — Respiration; photosynthesis (to be checked)
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: State Blackman's principle of limiting factors.
Interpret graphs of rate against light intensity, CO₂ and temperature.
Use the inverse-square law to compare light intensities and calculate rates.
reviewNotes: Curve values in the figure are illustrative, not measured data.
The inverse-square law assumes a point source in a dark room.
Syllabus references, scope and level of difficulty are to be checked against the official text; all facts, formulas and worked examples to be verified by a teacher before release.

blocks.title: Limiting factors
blocks.md: The **rate of photosynthesis** depends on **light intensity**, **CO₂ concentration** and **temperature** (and water, chlorophyll and mineral supply). The **limiting factor** is the one in shortest supply: increasing it increases the rate, but increasing other factors does not. On a graph, the part that rises shows the limiting factor on the x axis; the plateau shows that another factor has become limiting.

blocks.title: Reading the graph
blocks.md: Name the limiting factor **for each part** of the curve. On the rising part it is the factor being varied; on the plateau it is some other factor, which you should identify from the information given (for example, the curve with higher CO₂ concentration reaches a higher plateau, so CO₂ is limiting the lower curve). Temperature affects the enzymes: the rate rises with temperature, then **falls sharply** beyond about 40 °C as enzymes denature.

blocks.caption: Rate of photosynthesis against light intensity at two CO₂ concentrations.
blocks.alt: Two curves rising and levelling off, a lower blue curve for low CO₂ and a higher red curve for high CO₂.

blocks.title: In practice
blocks.md: An aquatic plant such as *Elodea* is illuminated by a lamp at measured distances; the rate is measured by counting bubbles of oxygen per minute or by a gas syringe. Light intensity is proportional to **1 ÷ d²** (inverse-square law). Keep temperature constant (e.g. with a water bath as heat shield) and CO₂ constant (add sodium hydrogencarbonate). In a greenhouse, growers raise CO₂ and temperature and use artificial light to increase yield.

blocks.title: Compensation point
blocks.md: At the **light compensation point** the rate of photosynthesis equals the rate of respiration, so there is no net exchange of CO₂ or O₂. Below it the plant loses carbon; above it the plant gains carbon and can grow.

blocks.title: Worked example — inverse-square law
blocks.statement: A lamp is moved from 10 cm to 20 cm from a plant. By what factor does light intensity change?
steps: The intensity at 20 cm is one quarter of that at 10 cm.

blocks.title: Worked example — rate from bubbles
blocks.statement: An Elodea shoot releases 36 bubbles in 3 minutes at 15 cm and 60 bubbles in 3 minutes at 10 cm. Calculate both rates and the % increase.
steps: Rate at 15 cm = 36 ÷ 3 = 12 bubbles per minute; at 10 cm = 60 ÷ 3 = 20.
